AU01.healthy: In a healthy adult face, the activation of AU01 results in the inner brow corners rising obliquely, with a peak amplitude of approximately 3-5 mm. This movement occurs rapidly, with an onset speed of around 100-150 ms, and is typically symmetrical across both sides of the face. The medial forehead furrows become pronounced above the glabella, and the movement smoothly returns to rest without any abrupt halts. The overall expression is dynamic and fluid, reflecting a natural and effortless brow raise.
AU01.parkinson: In a Parkinson's disease face, the activation of AU01 is characterized by a reduced amplitude, often diminished by 40–60% from the healthy baseline. The onset of the brow raise is delayed, typically by 150–300 ms beyond normal, and there may be noticeable left-right asymmetry exceeding 30%, compared to less than 10% in healthy individuals. The medial forehead furrows are less pronounced, and the movement lacks fluidity, often appearing rigid or incomplete. The most visually detectable difference is the significantly reduced amplitude and delayed onset of the inner brow raise, contributing to an overall expression of hypomimia.

AU02.healthy: In a healthy adult face, activation of AU02 results in the lateral portion of the frontalis muscle lifting the outer brow tail upward and outward. This movement creates subtle lateral forehead wrinkles that are approximately 2-3 mm in depth. The onset of this action is swift, occurring within 100-150 ms, and it is typically symmetrical across both sides of the face. The return to rest is smooth and controlled, with the brow descending back to its neutral position without any abruptness or hesitation.
AU02.parkinson: In a Parkinson's disease face, the activation of AU02 is characterized by a noticeable reduction in amplitude, with the outer brow tail lifting only 40-60% of the healthy baseline. The onset of this movement is delayed by 150-300 ms, and there is often a marked left-right asymmetry exceeding 30%, compared to less than 10% in healthy individuals. The lateral forehead wrinkles are less pronounced, and the return to rest may appear rigid and incomplete. The most visually detectable difference is the reduced amplitude and delayed onset of the outer brow lift, resulting in a less expressive appearance.

AU04.healthy: In a healthy adult face, activation of AU04 results in the corrugator supercilii and depressor supercilii muscles pulling the eyebrows downward and medially. This movement creates distinct vertical furrows in the glabella region, with a peak amplitude of approximately 3-5 mm. The onset of this action is rapid, occurring within 100-150 ms, and is typically symmetrical across both sides of the face. The return to rest is smooth, with the furrows gradually fading as the brows return to their neutral position.
AU04.parkinson: In a Parkinson's disease face, the activation of AU04 is characterized by a significant reduction in amplitude, often reduced by 40–60% from the healthy baseline. The onset of brow lowering is delayed by 150–300 ms, and there is often noticeable left-right asymmetry exceeding 30%, compared to less than 10% in healthy individuals. The vertical glabellar furrows are less pronounced, and the movement may plateau at only 50% of the full range. The most visually detectable difference is the diminished depth and asymmetry of the glabellar furrows, indicating early hypomimia.

AU05.healthy: In a healthy adult face, activation of AU05 results in the upper eyelid elevating smoothly, increasing the palpebral aperture by approximately 3 to 5 mm. The movement is rapid, with an onset speed of around 100 ms, and is typically symmetrical across both eyes. The levator palpebrae superioris muscle contracts efficiently, allowing for a full excursion that exposes more of the sclera. Upon deactivation, the eyelid returns to its resting position with a smooth and controlled descent, maintaining bilateral symmetry throughout the process.
AU05.parkinson: In a Parkinson's disease face, activation of AU05 shows a marked reduction in amplitude, with the upper eyelid elevating only 1 to 2 mm, reduced by 40–60% from the healthy baseline. The onset of movement is delayed by 150–300 ms beyond normal, and there is often noticeable left-right asymmetry, exceeding 30% compared to less than 10% in healthy individuals. The excursion is incomplete, with the eyelid plateauing at only 50% of its full movement range. The most visually detectable difference is the significantly reduced amplitude and delayed onset of eyelid elevation, resulting in less sclera exposure.

AU06.healthy: In a healthy adult face, the activation of AU06 results in the cheek mass elevating prominently, causing the lower eyelid to narrow and the outer canthus to crease, forming distinct crow's feet. The peak amplitude of the cheek elevation typically reaches 5-7 mm, with an onset speed of approximately 100-150 ms. The movement is bilaterally symmetrical, and the return to rest is smooth and fluid, with no abrupt halts. This action often accompanies a genuine smile, enhancing the expression's warmth and authenticity.
AU06.parkinson: In a Parkinson's disease face, the activation of AU06 is characterized by a noticeable reduction in the elevation of the cheek mass, with amplitude reduced by 40–60% from the healthy baseline. The onset of the movement is delayed by 150–300 ms, and there is often a marked left-right asymmetry exceeding 30%. The crow's feet are less pronounced, and the narrowing of the lower eyelid is minimal, resulting in a less expressive appearance. The most visually detectable difference is the significant reduction in the amplitude and symmetry of the cheek elevation, leading to a muted facial expression.

AU07.healthy: In a healthy adult face, activation of AU07 results in the lower eyelid margin moving upward, causing a slight narrowing of the palpebral aperture. The movement is smooth and symmetrical, with both eyelids rising approximately 2-3 mm. Onset speed is rapid, typically occurring within 100-150 ms, and the eyelids return to their resting position smoothly without any noticeable delay. This action is often accompanied by a subtle deepening of the nasolabial fold, contributing to a natural expression of intensity or concentration.
AU07.parkinson: In a Parkinson's disease face, activation of AU07 is characterized by a noticeable reduction in the upward movement of the lower eyelid margin, with amplitude reduced by 40–60% from the healthy baseline. The onset of the movement is delayed by 150–300 ms, and there is often a marked left-right asymmetry exceeding 30%, compared to less than 10% in healthy individuals. The eyelids may not achieve full closure, plateauing at only 50% of the normal movement range. The most visually detectable difference is the reduced amplitude and delayed onset, which contribute to a less expressive and more mask-like appearance.

AU45.healthy: In a healthy adult face, AU45 activation involves the orbicularis oculi muscle fully contracting to achieve complete bilateral eyelid closure. The palpebral aperture narrows swiftly, with an onset speed of approximately 100 ms, and the eyelids meet symmetrically at the midline. The peak amplitude of the closure is consistent, with the upper eyelid descending to cover the entire cornea. Upon reopening, the eyelids return to their resting position smoothly and effortlessly, maintaining a spontaneous blink rate of 12–20 per minute with minimal variation in amplitude or speed between blinks.
AU45.parkinson: In a Parkinson's disease face, AU45 activation is characterized by a marked reduction in blink frequency, with spontaneous blinks dropping to approximately 3 per minute. The onset of eyelid closure is delayed by 150–300 ms beyond normal, and the amplitude of closure is reduced by 40–60% from the healthy baseline, often resulting in incomplete eyelid contact. There is noticeable left-right asymmetry, with one eyelid frequently lagging behind the other, exceeding 30% asymmetry compared to less than 10% in healthy individuals. The most visually detectable difference is the significantly reduced blink rate, which serves as a sensitive early biomarker for Parkinson's disease.

AU09.healthy: In a healthy adult, activation of AU09 results in the nasal wings flaring laterally and upward, creating distinct 'bunny lines' across the nasal bridge. The peak amplitude of this movement can reach up to 3 mm, with an onset speed of approximately 150 ms. The movement is typically symmetrical across both sides of the face, and the return to rest is smooth and fluid, with no residual tension in the muscles involved. The nasolabial fold may deepen slightly as the upper lip elevates subtly in coordination with the nasal movement.
AU09.parkinson: In a Parkinson's disease patient, the activation of AU09 is characterized by a marked reduction in amplitude, often reduced by 40–60% from the healthy baseline. The onset of the movement is delayed by 150–300 ms beyond normal, and the frequency of spontaneous activation drops significantly from approximately 15 times per minute to about 3 times per minute. There is often noticeable left-right asymmetry, with one side of the nasal wings flaring more than the other. The most visually detectable difference is the reduced amplitude and delayed onset, leading to less pronounced 'bunny lines' and a more static appearance of the nasal region.

AU10.healthy: In a healthy adult face, the activation of AU10 results in the central upper lip elevating smoothly by approximately 3 to 5 mm. This movement is rapid, with an onset speed of around 100 ms, and is typically symmetrical across both sides of the face. The nasolabial folds deepen noticeably, and the upper teeth may become partially exposed. The return to rest is smooth and controlled, with no abrupt halting or jerking motions, maintaining a natural expression throughout the movement cycle.
AU10.parkinson: In a Parkinson's disease face, the activation of AU10 is characterized by a reduced amplitude, with the upper lip elevating only 1 to 2 mm, which is a reduction of 40–60% from the healthy baseline. The onset of this movement is delayed by 150–300 ms beyond normal, and there is often noticeable left-right asymmetry exceeding 30%. The nasolabial folds show minimal deepening, and the upper teeth are rarely exposed. The most visually detectable difference is the significantly reduced amplitude and delayed onset of the upper lip elevation.

AU12.healthy: In a healthy adult face, the activation of AU12 results in the lip corners being pulled upward and laterally by approximately 10-12 mm, creating a pronounced smile. The nasolabial folds deepen visibly, and the movement is typically symmetrical on both sides of the face. The onset of this action is rapid, occurring within 100-150 ms, and the return to rest is smooth and controlled. The zygomaticus major muscle engages fully, contributing to a dynamic and expressive facial expression.
AU12.parkinson: In a Parkinson's disease face, AU12 activation is markedly diminished, with lip corner movement reduced by 40–60% from the healthy baseline. The onset of the smile is delayed by 150–300 ms, and the nasolabial folds show minimal deepening. There is often a noticeable left-right asymmetry exceeding 30%, compared to less than 10% in healthy individuals. The most visually detectable difference is the significantly reduced amplitude and asymmetry of the lip corner movement, resulting in a less expressive and more rigid facial appearance.

AU14.healthy: In a healthy adult face, activation of AU14 results in the buccinator muscle contracting, causing the cheeks to compress inward. This action pulls the lip corners laterally, creating distinct dimples on the cheeks. The movement is typically symmetrical, with a peak amplitude of approximately 3-5 mm, and the onset speed is rapid, occurring within 100-150 ms. The return to rest is smooth, with the dimples gradually disappearing as the cheeks relax back to their neutral position.
AU14.parkinson: In a Parkinson's disease face, the activation of AU14 is characterized by a noticeable reduction in amplitude, reduced by 40–60% from the healthy baseline. The onset of the buccinator contraction is delayed by 150–300 ms beyond normal, and there is often a left-right asymmetry that exceeds 30%. The cheeks may not compress inward fully, resulting in a plateau at only 50% of the full movement range. The most visually detectable difference is the diminished and asymmetrical appearance of cheek dimples, which are less pronounced and slower to form compared to a healthy face.

AU15.healthy: In a healthy adult face, activation of AU15 results in the lip corners being pulled downward by approximately 3-5 mm, creating a distinct downward curve of the mouth. The movement is symmetrical on both sides, with an onset speed of around 150-200 ms. The skin below the lip corners is drawn down smoothly, and the mentolabial sulcus deepens slightly. The return to rest is fluid, with no abrupt halts, restoring the neutral position seamlessly within 200 ms.
AU15.parkinson: In a Parkinson's disease face, AU15 activation shows a marked reduction in amplitude, with the lip corners descending only 1-2 mm, reduced by 40–60% from the healthy baseline. The onset of movement is delayed by 150–300 ms, and there is often noticeable left-right asymmetry exceeding 30%. The skin below the corners appears less dynamically engaged, and the mentolabial sulcus shows minimal change. The most visually detectable difference is the significantly reduced amplitude and delayed onset of the downward lip corner movement.

AU20.healthy: In a healthy adult face, AU20 activation results in the lip corners stretching laterally, creating a horizontal vector across the face. The movement is typically symmetrical, with both lip commissures moving outward by approximately 5 to 7 mm. The onset of this action is rapid, occurring within 100 to 150 ms, and the return to rest is smooth and controlled. The nasolabial folds remain relatively unchanged, distinguishing this action from AU12, which involves an upward diagonal movement.
AU20.parkinson: In a Parkinson's disease face, AU20 activation shows a noticeable reduction in amplitude, with the lip corners stretching only 2 to 3 mm laterally, reduced by 40–60% from the healthy baseline. The onset of the movement is delayed by 150–300 ms, and there is often a marked left-right asymmetry exceeding 30%, compared to less than 10% in healthy individuals. The movement may plateau at only 50% of the full range, and the return to rest can appear jerky or incomplete. The most visually detectable difference is the significantly reduced amplitude and delayed onset of the lip corner stretch.

AU23.healthy: In a healthy adult face, the activation of AU23 results in the orbicularis oris muscle contracting, causing the lip margin to constrict and firm. This action produces a narrowed and slightly thinned outline of the lips, with the vermillion border becoming more defined. The movement is typically symmetrical, with a peak amplitude of approximately 2-3 mm, and occurs with an onset speed of around 100 ms. The lips return smoothly to their resting state without any residual tension or asymmetry.
AU23.parkinson: In a Parkinson's disease face, the activation of AU23 is characterized by a noticeable reduction in amplitude, reduced by 40–60% from the healthy baseline. The onset of lip tightening is delayed by 150–300 ms beyond normal, and there is often a marked left-right asymmetry exceeding 30%. Due to chronic perioral rigidity, the lips may appear perpetually constricted, with the dynamic range compressed and the lip outline less distinct. The most visually detectable difference is the persistent rigidity and reduced movement amplitude, leading to a less pronounced lip tightening effect.

AU24.healthy: In a healthy adult face, activation of AU24 results in the lips pressing firmly together, causing a noticeable thinning of the lip line. The lip commissures remain level, and the vermillion border is slightly accentuated as the lips protrude forward by approximately 2-3 mm. The onset of this movement is swift, occurring within 100-150 ms, and the action is symmetrically executed across both sides of the face. Upon release, the lips return smoothly to their resting position without any residual tension or asymmetry.
AU24.parkinson: In a Parkinson's disease face, AU24 activation is characterized by a marked reduction in amplitude, with lip protrusion reduced by 40-60% from the healthy baseline. The onset of lip pressing is delayed by 150-300 ms, and there is often a noticeable left-right asymmetry exceeding 30%, compared to less than 10% in healthy individuals. The lips may not fully press together, plateauing at only 50% of the full movement range, and the resting muscle tone is chronically elevated, limiting dynamic expression. The most visually detectable difference is the incomplete and asymmetrical lip pressing, which lacks the crisp definition seen in healthy faces.

AU25.healthy: In a healthy adult face, AU25 activation is characterized by a smooth and symmetrical parting of the lips. The lower lip depresses slightly, creating a gap of approximately 3-5 mm between the upper and lower lips. This movement occurs with a rapid onset speed of around 100-150 ms and returns to rest smoothly without any abruptness. The lip commissures maintain a balanced alignment, ensuring bilateral symmetry throughout the action.
AU25.parkinson: In a Parkinson's disease face, AU25 activation shows a noticeable reduction in amplitude, with the lip gap reduced by 40-60% from the healthy baseline. The onset of lip parting is delayed by 150-300 ms, and there is often a visible left-right asymmetry exceeding 30%. The movement may plateau at only 50% of the full range, and the return to rest can appear rigid and less fluid. The most visually detectable difference is the significantly reduced amplitude and delayed onset of lip separation.

AU26.healthy: In a healthy adult face, the activation of AU26 results in a noticeable lowering of the mandible, increasing the vertical dimension of the lower face. The movement is smooth and symmetrical, with the jaw dropping approximately 10-15 mm at peak amplitude. The onset of the movement is rapid, occurring within 100-150 ms, and the return to rest is fluid without any abrupt halts. The relaxation of the masseter and activation of the digastric muscle are well-coordinated, allowing for a full range of motion without any resistance or hesitation.
AU26.parkinson: In a Parkinson's disease face, the activation of AU26 is characterized by a significantly reduced jaw opening range, with the mandible lowering only about 4-6 mm, reduced by 40–60% from the healthy baseline. The onset of the movement is delayed by 150–300 ms beyond normal, and there is often a noticeable left-right asymmetry exceeding 30%. The return to rest may be jerky or incomplete, reflecting the rigidity and elevated resting muscle tone. The most visually detectable difference is the markedly reduced amplitude and delayed onset of the jaw drop, which diminishes the overall expressiveness of the lower face.

AU17.healthy: In a healthy adult face, activation of AU17 results in the chin boss pushing upward with a peak amplitude of approximately 3-5 mm. The skin over the chin becomes bunched, creating a distinct orange-peel texture as the mentolabial sulcus deepens. This movement occurs symmetrically across the midline with an onset speed of around 100-150 ms, and the return to rest is smooth and complete, restoring the chin's natural contour without residual tension.
AU17.parkinson: In a Parkinson's disease face, AU17 activation shows a reduced amplitude, typically diminished by 40–60% from the healthy baseline, resulting in a less pronounced upward push of the chin boss. The onset of movement is delayed by 150–300 ms, and the orange-peel texture is less distinct due to incomplete excursion, plateauing at only 50% of the full movement range. The mentolabial sulcus deepens minimally, and the return to rest is often sluggish, with residual tension visible. The most visually detectable difference is the significantly reduced amplitude and delayed onset, leading to a less dynamic and expressive chin movement.
